replacement.stem: Marisol, a payroll specialist at a biweekly-paid employer, is loading a new hire's dependent care assistance plan election of $6,500 for the plan year. Employees are paid every other Friday. What per-pay-period pre-tax deduction should Marisol set up?

$541.67, dividing the annual election by 12 months, which spreads the election across calendar months instead of scheduled paydays
$250.00, dividing the annual election by the 26 pay periods in a biweekly year
$325.00, dividing the annual election by 20 pay periods after excluding the six weeks in which a company holiday falls
replacement.explanation: A biweekly payroll has 26 pay periods (52 weeks divided by 2), so $6,500 divided by 26 equals $250.00 per period. The election amount the employee chooses drives the per-period math; the IRC Sec. 129 statutory exclusion ceiling is a separate figure that Congress adjusts (it moved for 2026) and it only caps how much may be sheltered, not how the deduction is spread. Option 0 uses 24, the semimonthly divisor, a classic confusion between biweekly and semimonthly frequency. Option 1 uses 12, treating the deduction as monthly when it is actually taken every other Friday. Option 3 invents a 20-period schedule; holidays shift pay dates but never reduce the number of biweekly periods. Watch for 27-pay-period years, where the employer must decide whether to prorate over 27 periods or hold the per-period amount and stop early.

$2,750, the excess over the $5,250 Section 127 exclusion for tax year 2026, added to federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare wages
$8,000, because the coursework was not job-related and Section 127 shelters only education that maintains or improves skills required in the employee's current position
$2,750, added to federal income tax wages only, since educational assistance above the exclusion is exempt from FICA

replacement.explanation: Section 127 requires a separate written plan, reasonable notice to eligible employees, and no discrimination in favor of highly compensated employees or owners. Within those conditions, assistance up to a per-employee annual ceiling is excluded from income tax and FICA wages; amounts above the ceiling are taxable wages unless the education is job-related and can be excluded instead as a Section 132(d) working condition fringe. Option 1 describes an individual return mechanism that has nothing to do with an employer exclusion. Option 2 is backwards: qualifying Section 127 assistance is excluded from both income tax and FICA wages. Because the dollar ceiling is a statutory figure that Congress changes and that is inflation-indexed for tax years beginning after 2026, payroll should pull the current-year amount from Publication 15-B rather than relying on a remembered number.

For tax year 2026, how much federal income tax should he withhold from the bonus?

$1,200, which is 24 percent of $5,000, applying the backup withholding rate to the payment
$1,850, which is 37 percent of $5,000, because the mandatory flat rate applies to any bonus paid on a separate check
$0 at the time of payment, because supplemental wages are trued up on the employee's return and are not subject to withholding when paid separately from regular wages

The optional flat rate is available only if the supplemental wages are identified separately from regular wages and the employer withheld income tax from the employee's regular wages in the current or prior calendar year; otherwise the aggregate method must be used. Option 1 uses 24 percent, which is the backup withholding rate for reportable payments to payees with a missing or incorrect TIN, not a wage withholding rate. Withhold 37 percent on the entire $200,000, because once cumulative supplemental wages pass $1 million the mandatory rate applies to the whole payment that crosses the line
Withhold 22 percent on the $40,000 that brings the year-to-date total to $1 million and 37 percent on the $160,000 above it
Withhold using the employee's Form W-4 and the aggregate method, because the mandatory flat rate applies only when the employer has no W-4 on file for the employee
replacement.explanation: The mandatory flat rate applies to supplemental wages in excess of $1 million paid to an employee during a calendar year, and for 2026 that rate is 37 percent. Renata splits the payment: $40,000 brings the year-to-date supplemental total to exactly $1 million and may be withheld at the 22 percent optional flat rate, and the $160,000 above the threshold must be withheld at 37 percent. Option 0 ignores the cumulative test, which looks at all supplemental wages paid during the year, not one check at a time. Option 1 overstates the rule by applying 37 percent to the pre-threshold portion as well. Option 3 is wrong on two counts: the mandatory rate cannot be waived by any W-4 election, and neither the aggregate method nor a W-4 entry may be used for the above-threshold portion. The $1 million threshold is statutory and is not indexed, but the 37 percent rate tracks the top individual rate, so confirm it in the current Publication 15.

Withholding is required on wages above $200,000 paid by this employer regardless of the employee's filing status, and any over- or under-withholding is settled on the couple's return

replacement.stem: Grace, a payroll coordinator, learns that several sales managers drive company-owned cars home and use them on weekends. Her CFO tells her nothing needs to be reported because the cars were inexpensive. How should Grace treat the personal-use miles?
options: The value of the personal use is a taxable fringe benefit that must be imputed to each driver's wages, regardless of what the vehicle cost
No imputation is required, because an employer-owned vehicle is a working condition fringe benefit whenever the employee also uses it for business
No imputation is required unless the vehicle's value exceeds the IRS ceiling for the cents-per-mile method, which is the dollar test for taxability
The employee deducts the personal-use value as an unreimbursed employee business expense, so payroll only needs to report total miles driven
replacement.explanation: Personal use of an employer-provided vehicle is taxable compensation subject to federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare, and the vehicle's cost has no bearing on whether it is taxable. Cost matters only for which valuation method is permitted: the cents-per-mile and fleet-average rules are available only when the vehicle's fair market value is at or below a ceiling the IRS adjusts every year, which is $61,700 for vehicles first made available in 2026. Option 1 overreaches on the working condition fringe, which shelters the business portion of the use, never the personal portion. Option 2 is the trap: it converts a valuation-eligibility limit into a taxability test. Option 3 relies on the unreimbursed employee business expense deduction, which TCJA suspended and P.L. 119-21 made permanently unavailable to employees. Only qualified nonpersonal use vehicles such as marked police cars and ambulances are excluded outright.

replacement.stem: To avoid large year-end withholding surprises on imputed vehicle income, Omar's employer elects under IRC Section 3402(s) not to withhold federal income tax on the value of employees' personal use of company cars. What is the payroll consequence of that election?
options: The value becomes nontaxable to the employee, because the election reclassifies the personal use as a working condition fringe benefit
The value is left off Form W-2 entirely, and the employee picks it up directly on the individual return

The value remains taxable wages and Social Security and Medicare tax must still be withheld; only federal income tax withholding is waived, and the employer must notify each affected employee of the election
The election waives federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare withholding, though the employer still owes its own share of FICA on the imputed amount
replacement.explanation: Section 3402(s) lets an employer elect not to deduct and withhold federal income tax on the value of an employee's personal use of an employer-provided highway motor vehicle. The election is narrow: the value is still wages, it must still appear on the employee's Form W-2, and Social Security and Medicare tax must still be withheld and matched. The election is conditioned on notifying the affected employee, generally by January 31 of the election year or within 30 days after the vehicle is first made available, and on the employer timely reporting the benefit on the wage statement. Option 0 confuses a withholding election with an exclusion from income. Option 1 would defeat the reporting condition the statute imposes. Option 3 extends the waiver to FICA, which the provision does not do, and then inconsistently keeps the employer share. Employers commonly pair this election with the special accounting rule for November and December benefits.

replacement.stem: Nadia receives a Form 668-W wage levy for an employee. The employee completes and returns the Statement of Dependents and Filing Status, claiming head of household with two dependents. How does Nadia determine how much of each paycheck is exempt from the levy?
options: She applies the ceiling that governs ordinary creditor garnishments, withholding 25 percent of disposable earnings and releasing the balance to the employee
She uses the amount derived from the employee's most recent Form W-4, since the levy exemption follows the employee's income tax withholding election
She remits the employee's entire net pay and lets the IRS refund the exempt portion directly, because a levy attaches to all wages until it is released

She looks up the exempt amount in the IRS Publication 1494 table issued for the current year, using the filing status and number of dependents the employee certified on the levy form, and remits everything above that amount
replacement.explanation: Publication 1494 converts filing status and number of dependents into a per-pay-period exempt amount built from the standard deduction and additional standard deduction amounts. Because those amounts are inflation-adjusted, the IRS reissues the table every year, so payroll must pull the current-year version rather than reuse a saved copy. Everything above the exempt amount goes to the IRS. Option 0 imports the Consumer Credit Protection Act's 25 percent cap, which by its terms does not limit federal tax levies. Option 1 uses the wrong form: the certification is made on the statement accompanying Form 668-W, not on Form W-4, and the two can differ. Option 2 ignores the exempt amount entirely. If the employee does not return the statement within three days, the exempt amount is computed as married filing separately with zero dependents, the least favorable result. The levy is continuous and stays in force until the IRS releases it on Form 668-D.

replacement.stem: Luis is running payroll for an employee who has been subject to an IRS wage levy for two months. A creditor garnishment for a credit card judgment arrives this week, and the collection agent insists on 25 percent of disposable earnings. After applying the levy, almost no pay remains. What should Luis do?
options: Split the available disposable earnings pro rata between the levy and the creditor garnishment so that neither order goes entirely unsatisfied
Satisfy the levy first, since it reaches everything above the Publication 1494 exempt amount, and remit nothing on the later creditor garnishment if no earnings remain
Satisfy the creditor garnishment first up to the 25 percent CCPA ceiling, then apply the levy to whatever disposable earnings are left
Withhold 25 percent for the creditor and cap the levy at 25 percent as well, so that no more than 50 percent of disposable earnings is taken in any period
replacement.explanation: A federal tax levy already in force when a creditor garnishment arrives has priority, and it reaches all pay above the Publication 1494 exempt amount. Title III of the Consumer Credit Protection Act does not limit federal tax levies, so there is no 25 percent ceiling to apply to the levy, and the later creditor order is honored only out of whatever remains, which is frequently nothing. Luis should return the creditor's answer form stating that no funds are available because of a prior federal tax levy. Option 0 invents a pro rata rule that no federal provision supports. Option 2 inverts the order of priority. Option 3 stacks two caps that do not exist for this pairing. The important exception to know: a child support withholding order already in effect when the levy arrives is honored first, and the IRS will generally reduce the levy to accommodate it.

replacement.stem: Bianca's employee is paid $10.00 per hour, worked 45 hours in a single workweek, and earned a $100 nondiscretionary production bonus attributable to that same week. What is the employee's FLSA regular rate for the week, and what additional overtime premium is owed?
options: $12.22 per hour, computed as $450 in straight time plus the $100 bonus divided by 45 hours, with an additional half-time premium of $30.56 for the 5 overtime hours
$10.00 per hour, with a $25.00 overtime premium, because a production bonus is a discretionary payment excluded from the regular rate
$12.22 per hour, with an additional premium of $91.67, computed as 1.5 times the regular rate for each of the 5 overtime hours
$11.11 per hour, computed as $500 divided by 45 hours, because the bonus is first allocated to the 5 overtime hours and then spread across all hours worked
replacement.explanation: The regular rate is all remuneration for the workweek divided by all hours actually worked: ($10.00 times 45 equals $450) plus the $100 bonus equals $550, divided by 45 hours equals $12.22. Because the $550 already compensates every hour at straight time, only the half-time premium remains on the overtime hours: $12.22 divided by 2 equals $6.11, times 5 overtime hours equals $30.56. Total owed for the week is $580.56. Option 1 treats the bonus as discretionary; a promised production bonus is nondiscretionary and must be included in the regular rate, while only bonuses whose fact and amount are left to the employer's sole discretion until at or near the end of the period may be excluded. Option 2 pays the full time-and-a-half on top of straight time that was already paid, double-counting the straight-time component. Option 3 misallocates the bonus to overtime hours; the bonus is spread over all hours the employee actually worked in the period it covers.

replacement.stem: In January 2026, Reggie's employer pays a nondiscretionary production bonus covering the 13 workweeks of the prior quarter. Several employees who share in the bonus worked overtime during some of those weeks. What must Reggie do?
options: Nothing beyond the tax step, since the bonus is supplemental wages and withholding at the optional flat rate satisfies the employer's obligations
Add the entire bonus to the workweek in which it is paid and pay a half-time premium on any overtime hours worked during that single week
Reallocate the bonus across the workweeks it covers, recompute the regular rate for each of those weeks, and pay the additional half-time premium on the overtime hours worked in each affected week
Exclude the bonus from the regular rate entirely, because it was calculated and paid after the work was performed, which makes it discretionary
replacement.explanation: A nondiscretionary bonus that covers more than one workweek must be apportioned back over the period it was earned. The employer recomputes each covered week's regular rate with that week's share of the bonus included, then owes an additional half-time premium on the overtime hours worked in each of those weeks. Where no better basis exists, the bonus may be allocated equally to each workweek or to each hour worked in the period. Option 0 confuses two independent obligations: withholding on supplemental wages settles the tax question and says nothing about wage-hour liability. Option 1 concentrates the entire bonus in the pay week, which overstates the premium for that week and pays nothing for the other twelve. Option 3 misstates the discretionary test, which turns on whether the employer retained sole discretion over both the fact and the amount until at or near the end of the period, not on when the check was cut; a promised production bonus is nondiscretionary no matter when it is paid.
